title: Q: Are we in the midst of cyberwar? A: Yes
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about a celebrity fan (Kristen Bell) and a young fan named Sam whose suggestions set the "Summer of Sam" topic list. The main topic is cyber war: the 1999 Olympic Pipeline explosion in Bellingham, Washington and SCADA control systems; US reliance on Windows and internet-connected infrastructure; Project Eligible Receiver, a Pentagon red-team exercise; Moonlight Maze, a Russia-traced espionage campaign against US agencies; US offensive cyber operations including the Serbia and Iraq attacks; types of attacks (Pearl Harbor-style, distributed denial of service, viruses like Code Red, Slammer, NIMDA); Stuxnet and Operation Olympic Games against Iran's centrifuges, with the related Flame malware; and defensive challenges, including private companies' security practices and Richard Clarke's views. The episode ends with a listener mail segment from a history professor about the Great Chicago Fire's effect on the beer industry and Milwaukee's Schlitz.

segments.title: Opening banter and Summer of Sam
segments.summary: Hosts mention Kristen Bell curating a Newsweek page and listening to the show, then introduce Sam, a young fan who sent topic suggestions that led to the Summer of Sam theme.

segments.title: Olympic Pipeline explosion and SCADA systems
segments.summary: A 1999 pipeline failure in Bellingham, Washington, controlled by a SCADA system, leaked gasoline, caused a fireball, and killed three people. Analysts later cited it as an example of what a cyber attack could do, though it was believed to be an accident. Hosts note that US companies, agencies, and infrastructure run on Microsoft Windows-based systems.

segments.title: Early warnings and Project Eligible Receiver
segments.summary: Hosts describe the Pentagon hiring a red team to test its defenses in Project Eligible Receiver, where hackers broke into Pentagon systems and it took three days for the Pentagon to notice.

segments.title: Moonlight Maze espionage
segments.summary: A year after the Eligible Receiver tests, an espionage campaign called Moonlight Maze spied on NASA, the Pentagon, and other agencies over about two years, gathering strategic maps and troop data. It was traced to Russia, though the origin was not certain. Hosts describe cyber warfare as already underway since the nineties, with optimists and pessimists about defense.

segments.title: US offensive cyber operations
segments.summary: Hosts note US use of computer attacks against Serbian air defenses during the Kosovo war and against Iraq in 2003. They discuss why Clinton and Bush reportedly declined to use viruses to drain terrorist bank accounts, citing the risk that such malware could be captured and reused against the US.

segments.title: Types of cyber attacks
segments.summary: Hosts describe a Pearl Harbor-style attack that is loud and sabotaging, distributed denial of service attacks that overwhelm servers with requests (such as the attacks on MasterCard linked to Anonymous), and viruses such as Code Red, Slammer, and NIMDA that spread quickly and can be triggered by timers or user action.

segments.title: Stuxnet and Operation Olympic Games
segments.summary: Stuxnet, a 2010 US and Israeli cyber weapon, was designed to sabotage Iran's uranium enrichment centrifuges. Hosts describe Operation Olympic Games, the CIA-led effort that studied the centrifuges, and the Flame malware that was reportedly introduced by thumb drive to map the system. Stuxnet made data look normal while centrifuges spun out of control, and it reportedly set Iran's program back by about a year.

segments.title: Defense challenges and private companies
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the US being connected to the internet as a vulnerability, the lag in US cyber defense compared with China and Russia, and security expert Richard Clarke's view that companies rush products to market without enough security testing. Strickland suggests education as a first step, and the hosts describe a possible combined cyber and physical attack on infrastructure.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts recommend Jonathan Strickland's article on cyber war and sign off.
